    Chapter 4

    Randomness: The Secret Ingredient

    🤔 A 256-bit key can secretly have the strength of a 15-bit one. Two deleted lines of code did exactly that to a whole operating system’s keys for two years.

    • ⏱️ ~5 min
    • 📚 5 sections
    • 🎮 3 interactive
    • ⭐ 200 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    4.1Why randomness matters so much#

    Every key, every password salt, every nonce must be unpredictable. If an attacker can guess how your key was generated, the strongest algorithm in the world won't save you.

    Think of it like a combination lock with a trillion combinations. If you always pick your birthday, the lock might as well have 365.

    💡 Key idea: A key is only as strong as the randomness used to create it. A 256-bit key generated from a predictable source might really have only 20 bits of security.

    ✔ section read

    4.2Three kinds of "random"#

    Type How it works Predictable? Used for
    True random (TRNG) Measures physical chaos: electrical noise, radioactive decay, timing jitter No Seeding (starting) the generators below
    Pseudo-random (PRNG) A formula that produces random-looking numbers from a starting value called a seed Yes, if you know the seed or see enough outputs Games, simulations, shuffling a playlist
    Cryptographically secure pseudo-random (CSPRNG) A PRNG built from crypto primitives, seeded with true randomness No, even after seeing lots of output Keys, nonces, salts, tokens — anything security-related

    Analogy: a normal PRNG is like a gigantic book of numbers. If you know which page you started on (the seed), you know every number that follows. A CSPRNG is a book that rewrites itself in a way nobody can predict, even after reading a thousand pages.

    📜 True story: lava lamps. The company Cloudflare has a wall of about 100 lava lamps in its San Francisco office. A camera photographs them, and the unpredictable blobs are mixed into its random number generators as an extra source of entropy. It's a fun, real example of turning physical chaos into randomness.

    Entropy is the measure of unpredictability, counted in bits. A fair coin flip gives 1 bit of entropy. A random 256-bit key has 256 bits of entropy. A password like password123 has close to zero, because it's one of the first guesses any attacker tries.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Random number generators compared

    👍 Situational
    TRNG

    Measures physical chaos

    • Genuinely unpredictable
    • Great seed material (even lava lamps!)
    • Slow and hardware-dependent
    • Can be biased without post-processing
    Best for: Seeding a CSPRNG
    ❌ Avoid
    PRNG

    A formula from a seed (e.g. Mersenne Twister)

    • Very fast
    • Reproducible: same seed, same sequence
    • Predictable after enough output (624 for MT)
    • Never safe for keys, tokens or salts
    Best for: Games, simulations, shuffling playlists
    ✅ Use it
    CSPRNG

    Crypto-built generator seeded with true randomness

    • Unpredictable even after seeing lots of output
    • Built into every OS and language
    • Must be seeded properly (early-boot devices failed)
    • Slightly slower than a plain PRNG
    Best for: Keys, nonces, salts, tokens: anything security-related
    ✔ section read

    4.3Where good randomness comes from#

    Your operating system collects unpredictable events (hardware noise, CPU randomness instructions, timing of interrupts) and feeds them into a CSPRNG. Always use it:

    Platform Use this Never use this for security
    Linux / macOS /dev/urandom, getrandom() —
    Python secrets module, os.urandom() random module
    JavaScript (browser) crypto.getRandomValues() Math.random()
    Node.js crypto.randomBytes() Math.random()
    Java SecureRandom java.util.Random
    Go crypto/rand math/rand
    Command line openssl rand $RANDOM

    ⚠️ Watch out: Python's random module uses an algorithm called the Mersenne Twister. After observing 624 of its outputs, an attacker can predict every future output. It's great for games and terrible for passwords or tokens.

    🧪 Try it yourself:

    Terminal
    # 32 random bytes as hex (64 characters) — a perfect AES-256 key
openssl rand -hex 32

# 24 random bytes as Base64 — handy for a strong random password
openssl rand -base64 24

# Straight from the operating system's generator
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | xxd -p -c 64
    Python
    import secrets
print(secrets.token_hex(32))       # random 256-bit value as hex
print(secrets.token_urlsafe(16))   # random token safe for URLs, e.g. password-reset links
print(secrets.randbelow(100))      # random number from 0 to 99

    4.4Nonces, IVs and salts: random helpers#

    Besides keys, cryptography uses a few other random-ish values. They're often confused, so here they are side by side:

    Term Plain meaning Must be secret? Must never repeat? Must be unpredictable? Where you'll meet it
    Key The secret that locks and unlocks ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Everywhere
    Nonce ("number used once") A value that makes each encryption unique, even with the same key and message ❌ No (sent openly) ✅ Yes, with the same key Not always (a counter can work) AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305
    IV (initialization vector) The starting value for some encryption modes ❌ No ✅ Yes ✅ Yes, for CBC mode AES-CBC
    Salt Random data mixed into a password before hashing, so identical passwords get different hashes ❌ No (stored next to the hash) ✅ Yes, unique per user Ideally Password storage (Chapter 8)

    Why would a nonce or salt not need to be secret? Their job isn't to hide anything. Their job is to make sure the same input never produces the same output twice. Remember lesson 3 from history: repetition leaks information.

    ✔ section read

    4.5When randomness fails: real disasters#

    📜 Debian OpenSSL (2006–2008). A developer removed two lines of code that a code-checking tool flagged as "using uninitialized memory." Those lines were feeding randomness into OpenSSL. For two years, Debian and Ubuntu systems could generate only about 32,768 different keys (based on the process ID number). Attackers could pre-compute all of them. SSH keys and certificates worldwide had to be replaced.

    📜 Sony PlayStation 3 (2010). The ECDSA signature algorithm needs a fresh random number for every signature. Sony used the same number every time. Hackers used two signatures to solve for Sony's private master key, which let anyone sign software as if they were Sony.

    📜 Android Bitcoin wallets (2013). A bug in Android's random number generator caused some wallet apps to reuse random values in signatures. Attackers computed the private keys and stole bitcoins.

    📜 "Mining your Ps and Qs" (2012). Researchers scanned the internet and found that tens of thousands of devices (routers, firewalls) had generated RSA keys right after booting, before they had gathered enough randomness. Many keys shared a prime factor, which let researchers instantly compute their private keys.

    📜 Dual_EC_DRBG (2006–2014). A random number generator approved as a US standard was later shown to likely contain a backdoor: whoever knew a secret relationship between its constants could predict its output. It was withdrawn in 2014.

    💡 Key idea: Always use your operating system's cryptographic random generator or a well-known library that uses it. Never invent your own, and never use a regular "random" function for anything security-related.
